cls: Peripheral vasodilator / lipid-modifying agent (inositol hexanicotinate, a 'no-flush' niacin ester)
pharm: Inositol nicotinate (inositol hexanicotinate) is an ester in which six molecules of nicotinic acid (niacin) are bound to one molecule of inositol; it is slowly hydrolyzed in the body to release free nicotinic acid and inositol, producing peripheral vasodilation and modest lipid-modifying effects with much less of the flushing typical of immediate niacin (hence 'flush-free' niacin).
quick: UK/SmPC: 3 g daily in divided doses (e.g., 1 g three times daily); range 2-4 g/day
Take with or after food to reduce gastrointestinal upset
Avoid unless clearly necessary; limited safety data
Avoid; insufficient data on milk transfer
Caution in renal impairment; limited data
Avoid in active liver disease; niacin metabolite is hepatotoxic
Avoid heavy use - additive flushing and hepatic risk
LFTs, glucose, uric acid with prolonged/high-dose use
summary: Inositol nicotinate (inositol hexanicotinate) is an ester of nicotinic acid and inositol used in some countries (notably the UK and parts of Europe) as a peripheral vasodilator for conditions such as intermittent claudication and Raynaud phenomenon, and historically as a lipid-modifying agent. It is marketed as a 'flush-free' or 'no-flush' niacin because it is hydrolyzed slowly to release nicotinic acid, blunting the prostaglandin-mediated flushing of conventional niacin. It is NOT approved by the US FDA; this record is derived from EMA/SmPC and BNF sources. The clinical evidence for meaningful benefit in peripheral vascular disease and dyslipidemia is limited and largely of low quality, and systematic reviews have not demonstrated convincing efficacy. Because it ultimately releases nicotinic acid, the same class cautions apply - flushing (less pronounced), hepatotoxicity, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, and GI upset - though typically milder at usual doses.
indications: Symptomatic relief in peripheral vascular disease, including intermittent claudication and Raynaud phenomenon (UK/SmPC indication)
Adjunct in the management of hyperlipidemia (historical use; limited evidence)

moa: Inositol nicotinate is the hexanicotinate ester of inositol. After oral administration it is absorbed and then slowly hydrolyzed by tissue esterases to liberate free nicotinic acid (niacin) and inositol. The gradual release of nicotinic acid produces peripheral vasodilation and the lipid-modifying actions characteristic of niacin (reduced hepatic VLDL/LDL output, raised HDL, lowered triglycerides) while largely avoiding the abrupt prostaglandin-mediated cutaneous flushing seen with immediate-release niacin, because plasma nicotinic acid concentrations rise slowly. The vasodilatory effect is thought to underlie its use in peripheral vascular disorders, although the clinical significance of these effects is uncertain.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to inositol nicotinate, nicotinic acid, or any component
monitor: Liver function tests with prolonged or high-dose use
Blood glucose in patients with or at risk of diabetes
Symptomatic response in peripheral vascular disease

preg: There is insufficient safety data for inositol nicotinate in pregnancy. As it releases nicotinic acid (whose pharmacologic doses are not recommended in pregnancy), avoid use during pregnancy unless considered essential and only after weighing potential benefit against risk. (Record derived from EMA/SmPC/BNF; not FDA-approved.)
lact: It is not known to what extent inositol nicotinate or its released nicotinic acid passes into breast milk at therapeutic doses. Because of limited data and the potential for adverse effects from nicotinic acid, avoid use during breastfeeding or discontinue nursing.
renal: Limited data in renal impairment. Use with caution; nicotinic acid and its metabolites are renally excreted and hyperuricemia may be more problematic with impaired renal function. Monitor as clinically appropriate.
hepatic: Because inositol nicotinate releases nicotinic acid, which can be hepatotoxic (particularly at higher cumulative doses), avoid use in active or significant hepatic disease and monitor liver function with prolonged or high-dose therapy. Discontinue if hepatic dysfunction or unexplained transaminase elevation occurs.

major: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) - potential additive risk of myopathy via released nicotinic acid
moderate: Antihypertensives and vasodilators - additive hypotensive/vasodilatory effect
Insulin and oral antidiabetic drugs - released niacin may raise blood glucose
Other hepatotoxic agents - additive liver risk
minor: Uricosuric/antigout drugs - released niacin may raise uric acid and blunt their effect
interactions.food: Take with or after food to reduce gastrointestinal upset; no specific food contraindication.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid heavy alcohol use, which can add to flushing and hepatic risk.
interactions.diagnostics: As with nicotinic acid, high doses may affect some urine catecholamine and glucose assays; monitor transaminases, glucose, and uric acid with prolonged use.

serious: Hepatotoxicity with prolonged or high-dose use (from released nicotinic acid)
emergency: Signs of hepatic dysfunction (jaundice, dark urine)

monitoring: Liver function tests with prolonged or high-dose therapy
Blood glucose, especially in diabetic or at-risk patients
Blood pressure if combined with other vasodilators
counsel: This medicine is taken to improve blood flow in the limbs or to help with circulation problems; take it with or after food
It is a 'flush-free' form of niacin, but you may still get mild warmth or redness of the skin, especially at higher doses
It can take several weeks to notice any benefit for circulation symptoms
Tell your doctor if you have liver disease, diabetes, or gout, as this medicine can affect them
Avoid heavy alcohol use, which can worsen flushing and stress the liver
Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, severe stomach pain, or unusual tiredness
This product is not approved by the US FDA; use it only under the guidance of your healthcare provider
pk: Gradual; vasodilatory and lipid effects develop slowly as the ester is hydrolyzed to nicotinic acid
Slow rise in plasma nicotinic acid (delayed compared with immediate-release niacin), reducing flushing
Determined by hydrolysis to and clearance of nicotinic acid (short half-life of the released niacin)
Sustained effect supporting 2-3 times daily dosing
Store at room temperature; keep dry and protect from light per the product labeling
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - this record is derived from EMA/SmPC and BNF sources; availability is mainly in the UK/Europe
Marketed as 'flush-free' / 'no-flush' niacin because slow hydrolysis to nicotinic acid blunts the prostaglandin-mediated flush
Evidence for efficacy is limited and largely low quality - systematic reviews have not demonstrated convincing benefit in intermittent claudication, Raynaud, or dyslipidemia
Because it releases nicotinic acid, the same class cautions apply (hepatotoxicity, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, GI upset) - monitor with prolonged or high-dose use
Do not assume it is interchangeable with prescription nicotinic acid lipid therapy; conventional lipid-lowering agents are preferred where lipid control is the goal
Usual UK dosing is 3 g daily in divided doses (range 2-4 g/day)
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for your next dose, in which case skip the missed dose and continue your normal schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose experience is limited. As inositol nicotinate releases nicotinic acid, excessive doses may cause flushing, gastrointestinal upset, hypotension, hyperglycemia, and potential hepatotoxicity. There is no specific antidote; management is symptomatic and supportive, with attention to blood pressure, hydration, and monitoring of liver function, glucose, and uric acid.
